positive: After some days spent in quiet solitude, during which we crossed many miles, we arrived at York, where we waited three hours for Alice.
negative: After some days spent in quiet solitude we arrived at York and waited three hours for Alice.
evidence: Days is the theme of spent and the temporal antecedent of during which. Strasbourg is the arrival destination and the antecedent of where, with Clerval awaited.

positive: Who could imagine the dangers of my private work while I dabbled among the dark recesses of the cellar or examined the wounded animal to revive the fragile body?
negative: Who could imagine the dangers of my private work and examine the wounded animal?
evidence: Who governs conceive and horrors is its object. Dabbled and tortured share the subordinate subject I. The purpose of torture is to animate the clay.

positive: She lifted the latch immediately, and they sat and shivered for a minute in the cold, alone in the cabin with the injured sailor's body.
negative: She lifted the latch immediately, and they sat in the cabin, where the injured sailor's body lay.
evidence: At once belongs to slipping the bolt. We controls the second pair; the duration and the dark modify panted. The captain possesses the body in the attendant circumstance.

positive: "No, madam, not we"; and immediately after she had uttered the phrase, I believe they all agreed with her.
negative: "No, madam, not we"; and I spoke to her after the others agreed.
evidence: The addressed negative reply excludes its self-subject. The perfect reporting event precedes the embedded agreement, whose subject is we and whose quantifier is all.

positive: Often, after that, we thought that he tried to talk even to us, in moments when they were left alone.
negative: Often, after that, we thought that he tried to talk to us alone.
evidence: The intervals attach to speaking, not the addressee me. Tried controls she, and the passive temporal relative belongs to intervals with we as its theme.

positive: Alice held a bag of provisions on her lap, which would have lasted them out comfortably, if they had been going to York by the same carriage.
negative: Alice held a bag of provisions on her lap, which was sore.
evidence: The basket is located on Peggotty's knee and is the antecedent of lasted, not the knee. The modal perfect lasting is conditional on the past-perfect progressive travel.

positive: Sadly, for we could not be there once again, and so near Helen, without the return of those memories with which we had so long been occupied.
negative: Sadly, for we could not return to Helen without the memories.
evidence: Here and near Agnes both predicate the subject under could not. The without-phrase sets the revival condition, and regrets is the antecedent of the pied-piped relative.

positive: After glancing at it for some seconds, she handed it to him, and said in a quiet tone, ‘Be so kind as take it, madam.’
negative: After glancing at it for some seconds, she handed it to him in silence.
evidence: The inspection precedes the giving. The same subject adds the direct request. Low voice is manner of added, and sir is the vocative within the request.

positive: They stopped; and followed the wooden coffin to a place we remember well, where the prayer was recited committing it to the earth.
negative: They stopped; and followed the wooden coffin to a place where we read the prayer.
evidence: The same overt We governs alighted and followed. Corner is the remembered place and locates the passive reading. The consignment is a nonfinite supplement with it as theme.

positive: Why hadn’t she mentioned, even the night before they went to school, that she thought she would be afraid, and she would rather not?
negative: Why did she mention that she would be afraid?
evidence: Hadn't is the negative perfect auxiliary of said in this inversion. I remains its overt subject. The day is a temporal incise, and rather not keeps an unresolved predicate in the report.

positive: After dinner, Dr. Martin retired to the study, as was his habit, and Helen went upstairs to her room.
negative: After dinner, Dr. Martin retired to the study, and Helen went upstairs to her room.
evidence: The custom parenthetical characterizes Bennet's retirement after tea. Mary's distinct stairs motion has its own destination.

positive: The ponies were hired; and neither the coach, nor the uniform of the driver who followed it, were familiar to us.
negative: The ponies were hired; and the uniform of the driver was familiar to us.
evidence: Post describes hired relay horses. The second copular predication has a coordinated negative subject. The servant is the subject of preceded and possessor of the livery.

positive: “There is, we suppose, in every character a tendency towards some distinct weakness--a natural flaw, which not even the best training can remove.”
negative: “There is in every character a flaw which training can remove.”
evidence: There is existential. I believe is an epistemic incise. The natural defect is the object of overcome, with education and the scalar negative scope under can.

positive: The visitors were rather more lucky, for they had the benefit of discovering from an open balcony that he wore a red jacket, and rode a grey pony.
negative: The visitors were rather more lucky, for they saw a horse from the open balcony.
evidence: The gain in fortune is explained by the ascertainment. The window frames the observing, and he wears a blue coat and rides a black horse in the embedded clause.

positive: Dr. Martin had not been in office three months, when he was tempted by an unexpected suggestion to look at York House.
negative: Dr. Martin had not yet been tempted to look at York House.
evidence: Had been of age is a negative perfect with two years as its measured duration. The linked when-clause has a passive temptation and a separately controlled looking complement.

positive: The latter was torn between admiration of the glow which sunlight had given to his face, and anxiety as to the situation's justifying her travelling so far alone.
negative: The latter was torn between admiration and anxiety about the glow.
evidence: Exercise gives the brilliancy to the complexion in an overt perfect relative. The second nominal contains occasion's justifying and its own lower possessive gerund her coming.

positive: We have promised that somebody should look for her and give her immediate warning if any strange vessel should appear in view.
negative: We have promised that somebody should look for her or remain at home.
evidence: The promise governs coordinated watching and giving with shared someone and should. The if-clause conditions both actions.

positive: "It gives us the greatest joy to meet you; but tell us how you found my mother, sisters, and Helen."
negative: "It gives us the greatest joy to meet you; but tell us where you found Helen."
evidence: Seeing you supplies the cause of the delight. In the imperative's embedded how-clause, how modifies left and father, brothers and Elizabeth are its coordinated objects.

positive: The doors of the hall had already been closed, and we sensed a sort of dread upon seeing the bright white light of the sun brighten the cabin.
negative: The doors of the hall had already been closed, and we saw the bright light.
evidence: The windows are the theme of the anterior passive. Panic is the felt affect; the lower visual predicate takes light as the overt subject of illuminate.

positive: From the bank where we then stood York was directly opposite, at the distance of a mile; and above it rose Hill Fort, in silent splendour.
negative: York Tower was opposite the bank, and we stood above it.
evidence: The source side is the locus of the where-relative. Montanvert is the predicand of opposite, and the postverbal Mont Blanc is the subject of inverted rose.

positive: We pointed to the place where she had vanished, and they followed the trail with dogs; ropes were thrown, but without success.
negative: We pointed to the place where she had vanished with the dogs.
evidence: Disappeared is relative to the spot, while boats are the means of following. Nets are the patient of the independent passive; in vain describes its failure.

positive: M. Martin was a tall thin man with a cold voice and a severe expression; the lecturer, accordingly, did not dispose us in favour of his studies.
negative: Martin was a tall thin man; the lecturer did not favour his studies.
evidence: M. is the honorific on Krempe. The second clause has its own overt teacher and scopes therefore and not over prepossess.

positive: "Ah," she snapped, "this’s it! Bring him inside quickly or I’ll seize your wrist."
negative: "Ah," she snapped, "bring him inside quickly."
evidence: Oh is the initial reported interjection. The next utterance has a separate identification and a directive whose or-clause presents the threatened alternative.

positive: And the following minute she and the sailor had jumped aboard of them, and they had pushed off and made way.
negative: And the following minute she and the sailor had jumped aboard of them, and they had pushed off.
evidence: The second had scopes both shoved off and given way. Its subject we is distinct from the two boarding participants in the first perfect.

positive: There was no noise except that of the distant waves, rising from below, and the buzz of tiny insects in the grass.
negative: There was no noise in the brush.
evidence: The negative existential has two coordinated exceptions, the sound of waves and the chirp. Mounting describes the distant breakers and in the brush locates the insects.

positive: Samuel withdrew from his seat in the cabin and jumped into the skiff, which we then took round to the vessel's stern, to be safer for Captain Morgan.
negative: Samuel withdrew into the cabin, which was safer for Captain Morgan.
evidence: The retreat and drop share Redruth. The boat is the goal and the object of the supplementary relative. The ship possesses the counter and handier predicates the boat in the purpose.

positive: She was confused; it seemed a favour so strange he was requesting--he, the old sailor, the leader throughout.
negative: She was confused; it seemed a request from the old sailor.
evidence: Asking is progressive and has an object gap linked to thing. The dash resumes its overt he and adds the buccaneer and ringleader appositions.

positive: "Yes, yes," answered Helen; "I remember her; she owed us money, she did, and carried my bag home with her."
negative: "Yes, yes," answered Helen; "she owed us money and carried my bag home."
evidence: Morgan reports two speech stretches. Did resumes owed rather than introducing a new lexical action. He also controls took, with knife as theme and ashore as goal.

positive: It was still rather late, and the darkest night that I think we ever were outside in--a silence that spread into the room.
negative: It was still rather late, and the darkest night I can remember.
evidence: The coldest morning is the temporal description and the antecedent of stranded in. Abroad predicates the relative subject, and the dash introduces the marrow-piercing chill as an elaboration.

positive: We would suppose he might have been as much as five metres tall.
negative: We would suppose he was tall.
evidence: The inner copula is modal perfect, with it as predicand. As much as and seven feet measure high. Should belongs to the matrix epistemic predicate.

positive: ‘All of a tremble,’ said Dr. Martin, imitating that expression and making her hands tremble.
negative: ‘All of a tremble,’ said Dr. Martin, as her hands trembled.
evidence: Shiver is the reported fragment. The reporter controls the two participles. His teeth are both the causee of making and the subject of bare chatter.

positive: We declared that no one else should move it; and this gave Alice such joy that she walked home in high spirits.
negative: We insisted that Alice should move it, and she walked home in high spirits.
evidence: Nobody else scopes the modal touch. The second clause states the degree-result relation between delight and going away. Away belongs to went.

positive: ‘Ah dear me, dear me, do you believe it might do us some harm?’ cried his sister in an anxious tone.
negative: ‘Do you believe it might do us some harm?’ cried his sister in an anxious tone.
evidence: Oh and the repeated dear me precede a do-supported question. The content has a distinct lexical do with good as effect, and the helpless manner belongs to cried.

positive: She was sitting close behind him, with one of her bare hands against her cheek, and the other lying on the teacher's desk.
negative: She was sitting close behind him, with both hands on the teacher's desk.
evidence: The progressive posture has two accompanying absolutes, one locative and one participial. One and the other select members of the same hand set.

positive: ‘Thank you, Captain Morgan,’ answered Helen, placing her letter down upon the table--‘I think you stay there, some time, Captain Morgan?’
negative: ‘Thank you, Captain Morgan,’ answered Helen, placing her letter down upon the table.
evidence: Both title-name occurrences are vocatives in their own utterances. The reporting phrase controls the putting-away gesture, while stop has its own location and duration.

positive: After lunch, the following day, she had set her book aside, and was walking out of the hall, when Dr. Martin called her inside.
negative: After lunch she left the hall and Dr. Martin called her inside.
evidence: Had attaches to put in the first predication. Was is the progressive of going, which shares I and is interrupted by the other subject's call.

positive: That young clerk, hired in a fortunate hour at five pounds two per year, was a cause of frequent annoyance to us.
negative: That young clerk was a cause of annoyance to us.
evidence: Page denotes the hired attendant, not a document. The supplement encodes a predecimal rate, with the source ten as the implied shilling amount. The main copula introduces the source of trouble.

positive: That was, to wait beside the hedge near the side of her old house, in a spot where there used to be a shed.
negative: That was, to wait beside the hedge while she went home.
evidence: The copula identifies an infinitival plan. The wall has its own location, while the corner locates lying and heads the past habitual existential relative.

positive: He imagined himself the focus of admiration, to dozens and to hundreds of them at present unfamiliar.
negative: He imagined himself giving attention to dozens of people.
evidence: Herself is the reflexive object and predicand of object of attention. The audience is quantified under to tens and scores, with at present anchoring their unknown status.

positive: “We suppose he will. He is now about Mr John Morgan’s height, or rather shorter.”
negative: “We suppose he will. He is now taller.”
evidence: The first prediction has unresolved verb ellipsis. In the next clause the genitive names the height benchmark, and or rather taller corrects that comparison rather than apposing a noun.

positive: “Maybe it would be better if we prevent her going there so very frequently. In any case, we must not remind his father of asking them.”
negative: “Maybe it would be better if we prevent her. In any case, we must not remind his father.”
evidence: The possessive gerund his coming is the object of discourage, with here and the degree-frequency expression inside it. Should not scopes remind in the separate utterance.

positive: Helen longed to remark that Dr. Martin had been a very charming companion; so readily guided that his value was immense; but she restrained herself.
negative: Helen longed to remark that Dr. Martin had been a charming companion, but she restrained herself.
evidence: Had attaches to been in the embedded content. Bingley is the predicand and the patient of the reduced guided supplement. Elizabeth controls observe and the final self-restraint.
